subtype: Safety and consent in sharing images and voice [Regulating]
passage: I'm Vasudha. At my cousin's engagement I recorded a voice note of Parul singing in the kitchen, and I nearly posted it to our family group because it was so sweet. Then I stopped, because she hadn't said yes. I messaged her: "Your song is lovely. Can I share it with the family group? Totally fine if you say no." A minute later she wrote, "Please don't, I sounded croaky. Keep it just for us." I deleted the draft. Weeks after that, a man I had met online kept asking me for photos and said everyone does it. I remembered that I could say no, and I did. I told my elder sister, and she helped me block him. I would have been the one hurting Parul if I had posted first.

qa.q: What did Vasudha ask Parul before sharing the voice note?
qa.a: She asked whether she could share it with the family group, and said it was fine if Parul said no.

qa.q: What was Vasudha thinking when she stopped before posting the voice note?
qa.a: She realised Parul had not said yes, so it was not hers to share, and she did not want to hurt her.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do when the man online kept asking for photos?
qa.a: She said no, told her elder sister and blocked him.

qa.q: Why might Parul have refused to have her song shared?
qa.a: She felt she sounded croaky, so she may have been embarrassed, and it was her right to say no.

grounding: A young adult asks before sharing another person's voice note, and refuses and reports pressure to send photos to a trusted person.

subtype: Safety and consent in sharing images and voice [Regulating]
passage: Note from Gargi, team lead. At the offsite Neelam took the group photos. Before uploading each to the shared album she asked the people in it, "Is this one okay to share?" One colleague said no to a photo of them mid-yawn, and Neelam deleted it there and then. Later she told me a stranger on a social platform had been pressing her for private pictures. She felt uneasy but wasn't sure she was overreacting. I told her she was right to be uneasy and that nobody is entitled to her images. We went through how to report the account to the platform, and I suggested she tell her family too. She agreed to keep the messages in case she wanted to show them. There is no blame on her.

qa.q: What did Neelam do with the photo the colleague refused?
qa.a: She deleted it there and then.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling about the stranger's messages?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and was unsure whether she was overreacting.

qa.q: What steps did Gargi suggest to Neelam?
qa.a: To report the account to the platform, tell her family and keep the messages in case she wants to show them.

qa.q: How might the colleague have felt when Neelam asked about the yawning photo?
qa.a: Respected, because they were asked and their no was accepted straight away.

grounding: A young adult asks before sharing others' photos, and pressure to send private pictures is reported to a trusted person, seen by a team lead.

subtype: Storytelling at work and in public [Regulating]
passage:
Tuesday. Manjula had to present the quarterly plan to forty colleagues, and her hands shook when she read her slides aloud to the mirror. Shreya, her friend from finance, said, "Tell me a story, not a list."
Thursday. Manjula practised with a one-minute story about a customer who had waited three weeks for a refund, and rehearsed a pause after the line "nobody called her back." She timed it and marked where to slow down.
Friday. In the hall her heart pounded, but she began with the customer. When she said, "Nobody called her back," she waited two full seconds. The room went quiet. Afterwards Shreya said, "I got goosebumps. Check the numbers though; that story doesn't prove the whole plan." Manjula nodded and added the figures to the appendix.

qa.q: How long had the customer waited for a refund?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling on Tuesday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was nervous, since her hands shook when she read her slides aloud to the mirror.

qa.q: Why did Shreya add "Check the numbers"?
qa.a: A moving story can persuade beyond the evidence, so figures are needed to show whether the plan is sound. 🙂

qa.q: How might the audience have felt during the pause?
qa.a: The quiet suggests attention and perhaps a pang for the customer, though we cannot know each person's reaction.

grounding: A young professional shapes a talk with a story, pacing and pauses, moderates nerves through practice, and checks content because a story can mislead.

subtype: Storytelling at work and in public [Regulating]
passage: Nikita, you're dreading the town-hall talk? Sit. I'm Gautam. At twenty-five I had to explain the plant's new safety routine to two hundred workers, and I thought facts would do it. I read a list. Half the hall stared at their shoes. My supervisor took me aside and said, "Tell them about Ramesh's hand." Next time I told the true story of a man who lost two fingers to a guard that wasn't in place, slowly, with a pause before his name. You could hear the fans. I practised it eight times the night before, and my knees still shook, but the shaking made me slow down. One warning though: a good story can carry a weak argument. Check that the story is true and stands for the facts.

qa.q: How many times did Gautam practise the story the night before?
qa.a: Eight times.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he told the story, and how did it help?
qa.a: His knees shook from nerves, but that made him slow down, which suited the pause.

qa.q: What could Nikita do for her town-hall talk?
qa.a: She can pick one true story, rehearse it with pauses and check that it fits the facts.

qa.q: How might the workers have felt when Gautam read the list, compared with the story?
qa.a: With the list they stared at their shoes, so they were bored or unmoved; with the story the quiet suggests they listened closely.

grounding: A young professional learns to move an audience with a story, pacing and pauses, and to check that a persuasive story matches the facts.

subtype: Craft and symbolic objects in rituals [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Kalyani, and I used to think a diya was only for Diwali, all joy and sweets. Last year my friend Ritu invited me to her father's first memorial day. In the living room stood his photo with a garland, and in front of it a single diya, lit at dawn and kept burning. The house was quiet. The same little flame that meant a party in my home meant remembering there. I almost said "how pretty," then stopped, because Ritu's face was tight. I asked, "What does the diya mean to you today?" She said, "It's how we keep him with us." I sat in front of it for a while. Months later, at Diwali, Ritu laughed as she lit a row of them on my balcony.

qa.q: What stood in front of the photo in Ritu's living room?
qa.a: A single diya, lit at dawn.

qa.q: What was Kalyani thinking when she noticed Ritu's tight face?
qa.a: She realised the diya had a solemn meaning there, unlike the party meaning in her home, and did not want to be careless.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do at a ritual she does not know?
qa.a: She can ask gently what the object means to the family and follow their lead.

qa.q: How is the same diya different for Ritu's household?
qa.a: It is a way of keeping her father with them, and not a celebration.

grounding: The same lit diya is joyful at Diwali and sombre at a memorial, so cultural context and the family's meaning define it.

subtype: Craft and symbolic objects in rituals [Mismatch]
passage: Neelam here, from the flat opposite. On the morning of the housewarming downstairs, Swati drew a large rangoli of petals with a lit diya at Mrs. Rao's door. Everyone smiled. That afternoon she climbed to Ketaki's flat, where the family was in mourning, carrying the same bowl of petals. She stood at the door a moment, then set the bowl down and rang the bell. "I brought petals, but I don't know if you'd want them today," she said. Ketaki's mother answered, "Not at the door. But you can put a few near his photo." Swati laid three petals by the photo, quietly. I couldn't tell whether the family found it comforting or simply polite.

qa.q: Where did Swati draw the rangoli?
qa.a: At Mrs. Rao's door.

qa.q: What might Swati have been thinking as she stood at the door with the petals?
qa.a: That petals which were joyful downstairs might not be welcome in a house in mourning, so she was careful and asked.

qa.q: What did Swati do that showed respect?
qa.a: She asked before putting anything at the door and followed the family's answer.

qa.q: How might Ketaki's mother have felt about the petals?
qa.a: Perhaps touched by the care, or simply politely accepting; Neelam cannot tell.

grounding: A young adult uses petals and a rangoli to mark meaning, joyful at a housewarming and sombre at a house in mourning, and asks the family.

passage: Seema, you sent your team lead a clapping GIF after she changed the deadline, and now she's gone quiet? I'm Leela, and I did the same at your age. My manager cancelled my leave and I replied with a sticker of a smiling cat saying "Fine!" I meant it as a small joke. He read it as sarcasm and it hurt him. Among my friends that sticker was warm and silly; to him it was a slap. It took a phone call to fix. Now, when the stakes are high, I write words: "I'm disappointed about the leave. Can we find another option?" Stickers are for when I know how they'll land.

qa.q: What sticker did Leela send her manager?
qa.a: A sticker of a smiling cat saying "Fine!"

qa.q: What did Leela intend by the sticker?
qa.a: She meant it as a small joke, though it landed differently, so intent and effect can differ.

qa.q: What could Seema do about the clapping GIF?
qa.a: She can call or write a short plain message explaining what she meant and check how it landed.

qa.q: How did Leela's manager read the sticker?
qa.a: As sarcasm that hurt, unlike Leela's friends, who found it warm and silly.

grounding: The same sticker can be warm or sarcastic depending on the relationship, so tone needs checking when stakes are high.

passage: The signal on the factory floor was so weak that Kashish could send only one-line messages. Sachin, her project lead, wrote, "We need to redo the sample tonight." She was tired and already annoyed, and she sent back a single 🙂. She meant "okay, understood." Sachin, reading it in his warm office, saw a forced smile, the kind people make while hiding annoyance. He typed, "Are you upset?" but the message would not send. He stood up and phoned the site office. Kashish took the call outside, where the signal held. "The smile was just yes," she laughed tiredly. "But I am tired, honestly." Sachin said, "Then let's move the sample to the morning."

qa.q: What did Kashish send back to Sachin?
qa.a: A single 🙂.

qa.q: What was Sachin thinking when he saw the smile?
qa.a: He thought it was a forced smile hiding annoyance, though Kashish meant it as yes.

qa.q: What could they do when the stakes are high?
qa.a: Use words or a call to check tone, as Sachin did by phoning.

qa.q: How might Kashish have felt when Sachin phoned?
qa.a: Relieved to be asked and able to say she was tired.

grounding: The same smiling emoji can be warm or passive-aggressive, so tone was checked by a call when stakes were high and the signal was weak.

passage:
Pallavi: Met the new client today. Suit, gold watch, sunglasses on his head. Total show-off 😅
Uday: lol why
Pallavi: Who wears that to a warehouse meeting
Uday: Did he say something rude?
Pallavi: No... he actually asked the loaders their names
Uday: Hmm
Pallavi: He said the watch was his father's and he wears it for luck. And the suit is because it's his first big meeting
Uday: So you judged the watch before you asked
Pallavi: Fair. I assumed money and attitude
Uday: Ask next time, "nice watch, is there a story?" 🙂
Pallavi: Good line. Feeling a bit silly now

qa.q: Whose watch did the client say it was?
qa.a: His father's.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling at the end of the chat?
qa.a: A bit silly, since she realised she had assumed things from his look.

qa.q: What could Pallavi ask next time?
qa.a: Something like "nice watch, is there a story?"

qa.q: How might the client have felt if she had voiced her first guess?
qa.a: Judged or unwelcome, especially at his first big meeting.

grounding: A person guesses wealth and attitude from clothes and accessories, the guess is wrong, and respectful curiosity is the better response.

passage: At the small-town bus stand, Anand watched a woman step off the bus in jeans and a short haircut, carrying a steel toolbox. "City girl, lost," he thought, and offered to point her to the taxi stand. "Thanks, but I'm here for the Patil farm," Disha said. "Their buffalo has a hoof problem." Anand blinked. She was the new veterinary officer, and she had grown up two villages away. He felt his face burn. "Sorry, I assumed," he said. Disha smiled, half tired, half amused. "I get that often. Which way is the Patil farm?" Anand walked her there, asked about her work on the way, and listened.

qa.q: What was Disha carrying?
qa.a: A steel toolbox.

qa.q: What did Anand feel when he learned who Disha was?
qa.a: He was embarrassed, since his face burned, because his guess from her clothes and hair was wrong.

qa.q: What could Anand do differently next time?
qa.a: He can ask an open, respectful question first, like whether he can help her find something, without deciding who she is.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt about being mistaken for a lost city girl?
qa.a: Tired and amused, as she says it happens often, though it may also be wearing.

grounding: A person guesses a stranger's background from clothes and hair, is wrong, and moves to respectful curiosity.

passage: Sumit, you say a man in a crisp uniform and a lanyard came to your flat asking to check the meter and for your card details? Hear what happened to me. I'm Mridul. At twenty-five a man in a khaki shirt and a badge rang my bell and said he was from the power company and needed my bill and an OTP to "fix an error." The uniform looked right and my first thought was to trust him. But something nagged me: a real officer wouldn't need an OTP. I said, "Please wait, I'll call the power company's number from my bill." He said he'd come back later and left quickly. The helpline confirmed no visit was planned. Anyone can buy a shirt and print a badge. Check through the official number, not the one they give you.

qa.q: What did the man ask Mridul for besides checking the meter?
qa.a: His bill and an OTP.

qa.q: What was Mridul thinking when the man asked for an OTP?
qa.a: He felt something nag him, since a real officer wouldn't need an OTP, even though the uniform looked right and he first wanted to trust it.

qa.q: What should Sumit do now?
qa.a: He should not share details, check through the official number on his bill or website, and tell a trusted person.

qa.q: How might the man have reacted to Mridul's plan to call?
qa.a: He left quickly, which suggests he did not want the check, though that is not proof.

grounding: A uniform and badge signal a role, but identity must be verified through the official channel because anyone can wear a costume.

passage: Rain was pouring and the lobby was closing in ten minutes when a man in a delivery uniform and a lanyard hurried to Tanvir's security desk. "Urgent parcel for the sixth floor, Damini Rao. I have to hand it to her myself," he said, dripping. The uniform looked right and the man looked tired, and Tanvir felt a pull to wave him through. Instead he said, "Sorry, I'll call her first." He dialled Damini's extension. "A parcel?" she said. "I didn't order anything. Don't send him up; I'll come down." The man said, "Never mind, wrong address," and walked back into the rain. Tanvir didn't know whether the man had been a scammer or just mistaken. He wrote the time and description in the visitor log.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do first at the desk?
qa.a: He said he would call Damini first, then dialled her extension.

qa.q: What was Tanvir feeling when he saw the man in the delivery uniform?
qa.a: He felt a pull to wave him through, out of sympathy for a tired, wet man, but he still chose to check.

qa.q: Why was calling Damini a good step?
qa.a: It verified the claim through a proper channel, since anyone can wear a uniform.

qa.q: How might the delivery man have felt when he was refused?
qa.a: Perhaps frustrated or embarrassed, or simply mistaken; Tanvir could not tell.

grounding: A young professional reads a uniform and lanyard as a signal of role but verifies through the proper channel despite time pressure and bad weather.

passage: Friday, 10:30 pm. Presentation day, Simran. When I finished the vendor pitch, the room clapped. Fast, loud, a couple of whistles, and I thought, yes! Then Rekha, my manager, clapped just twice, slowly, looking at her phone. I couldn't stop replaying it. Was it approval? Boredom? Rekha never claps much, and at last month's town hall she clapped the same way for the director's speech. Later she said, "The pricing slide was sharp. Send it to me?" So maybe it meant "I'm thinking," not "not good." Still, I wish I had asked instead of stewing all evening. Tomorrow I'll ask her directly.

qa.q: How many times did Rekha clap?
qa.a: Twice, slowly.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling as she replayed the applause?
qa.a: Uneasy and unsure, since the room's loud clapping felt good but Rekha's slow two claps left her wondering.

qa.q: What could Simran do to find out what Rekha thought?
qa.a: She can ask her directly for feedback, as she plans to do tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Rekha see her own clapping?
qa.a: Possibly as her usual style, since she claps the same way for the director's speech, and not as a sign of disapproval. 🙂

grounding: The same sound of applause, loud from the room and two slow claps from a manager, can mean approval, courtesy or something else.

passage:
Sangeeta: Did you see the team channel? Everyone sent 👏 after my update
Gopika: I saw. Two of them were Karan and Ali, who send that to everything 😅
Sangeeta: Ha. And Meera sent a row of four 👏 with no text. Is that warm or sarcastic?
Gopika: Hmm. Meera did the same when the server crashed last week, and she wasn't happy then
Sangeeta: That's what I'm worried about
Gopika: Just ask her? "Thanks, was that a good update or did I miss something?"
Sangeeta: Feels awkward
Gopika: Less awkward than guessing all week
Sangeeta: Fine, sending now

qa.q: What did Meera send after Sangeeta's update?
qa.a: A row of four 👏 with no text.

qa.q: What is Sangeeta worried about?
qa.a: That Meera's repeated claps might be sarcasm, as they seemed to be when the server crashed.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta ask Meera?
qa.a: She can ask, "Thanks, was that a good update or did I miss something?"

qa.q: How might Meera see her own claps?
qa.a: Possibly as warm support, or as tired sarcasm; without asking, nobody can tell.

grounding: The same clapping emoji can be approval, courtesy or irony, so tone is checked by asking.

passage:
Saturday. Vasudha went to a street festival with Parul. The crowd near the stage was thick, and chants started from two groups of young men on opposite sides. She felt shoulders pushing. She squeezed Parul's hand and said, "Let's move to the edge, near the tea stall." They stepped out before it got worse.
Wednesday. On the phone, Parul said the chants had turned into shoving twenty minutes after they left. Vasudha felt a shiver and was glad. She wrote down a rule: know the exit, stay near the edge.
Next Sunday. At a football match, when a group behind her began shouting at another, Vasudha didn't turn or shout back. She and Parul chose the aisle seats, kept their voices low and walked out at half-time.

qa.q: Where did Vasudha suggest they move to?
qa.a: To the edge, near the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she felt shoulders pushing?
qa.a: She felt anxious and alert, since she squeezed Parul's hand and decided to move.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do differently at the football match?
qa.a: She chose aisle seats, kept her voice low, ignored the shouting and left at half-time.

qa.q: How might Parul have felt when Vasudha suggested moving?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised at leaving the festival, but she went along, and later she may have been relieved on hearing about the shoving.

grounding: A young adult notices rising chants and pushing in a crowd, stays calm, keeps an exit, avoids provoking anyone and steps away.

passage: Hansa, you say you're going to the rally on Sunday and your mother is worried? Let me tell you what I saw at twenty-four. I'm Santosh. It was a festival procession, and the crowd was happy until two groups began shouting at each other. The chants got louder and faster, and people started pushing towards the front. My friend wanted to stay and film. My heart was thumping, but I kept my voice calm and said, "Let's go to the side lane now." We slipped out the way we had come in, walking, not running. A few minutes later a bottle was thrown. I never argued with the shouters or answered back. Know your exit before you need it.

qa.q: Where did Santosh suggest they go?
qa.a: To the side lane.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling while the chants got louder?
qa.a: His heart thumped, so he was alarmed, but he kept his voice calm.

qa.q: What could Hansa do before the rally?
qa.a: She can note the exits, stay near the edge, tell a family member where she will be and leave if pushing starts.

qa.q: How might Santosh's friend have felt about leaving?
qa.a: Disappointed at missing the filming, since the friend wanted to stay, though leaving kept them safe.

grounding: A young adult in a tense procession notices rising chants and pushing, keeps calm, avoids provoking anyone and leaves through an exit.

passage: In Nairobi, Esther saw her feed fill with a hashtag and black profile pictures after a factory fire on the outskirts killed several workers. She changed hers too and shared the petition link. It took thirty seconds, and she felt she had done something. By evening the feed had moved on to a football match. Her friend Abebe messaged, "Did you sign? Also, my church is collecting blankets and food for the families on Saturday. Want to come?" Esther paused, a little embarrassed at how quickly she had moved on. "Yes," she wrote. "I'll bring rice and come at nine." On Saturday they packed boxes together. The black picture had faded from most feeds by then, but the boxes were real.

qa.q: What did Abebe's church collect?
qa.a: Blankets and food for the families.

qa.q: What was Esther feeling when Abebe messaged her?
qa.a: A little embarrassed at how quickly she had moved on, but ready to act.

qa.q: How can online solidarity be made more useful?
qa.a: By pairing it with real support, like helping pack and deliver goods.

qa.q: How might the families see the online posts compared with the boxes?
qa.a: The posts show that people care, but the boxes give practical help; they would likely value both. 🤍

grounding: A young adult joins a hashtag and petition to show solidarity, and pairs it with real support because digital unity is easy and quick to fade.

passage: In the university lab, the group chat lit up with a flood hashtag and black-square profile pictures after news came of floods near a labmate's hometown. Irfan changed his picture and typed, "Solidarity with everyone affected." Within minutes twenty replies of hearts followed, and then silence. Pooja, at the next bench, looked at her phone and then at Irfan. "Nice. Should we also ask Ishan what his family needs before we send anything?" she said. Irfan felt a small flush. He asked Ishan, who said dry rations and boats for the village helped, through a local fund his uncle trusted. By evening the lab had collected a small amount and posted the receipt in the chat. Irfan said, "Posting was the easy part."

qa.q: What did Pooja suggest asking Ishan?
qa.a: What his family needs before sending anything.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when Pooja spoke?
qa.a: A small flush of embarrassment, realising the post alone was the easy part.

qa.q: What made the lab's response more useful?
qa.a: They asked what was needed, gave through a fund trusted locally and shared the receipt.

qa.q: How might Ishan have felt seeing the chat?
qa.a: Touched by the care, but probably most helped by the practical support.

grounding: A young adult shows solidarity online with a hashtag, and colleagues pair it with real support after asking what is needed.

subtype: Affectionate and delighted at work and home [Regulating]
passage: Note from Kalyani, team manager. Ritu is warm without crowding people. When Anil's proposal was approved she was first to say, "This is brilliant, you must be so pleased!" in a bright voice, and she organised a small tea break for everyone. She thanks colleagues by name in emails. With a new colleague who seemed uneasy about hugs, she offered a namaste and moved on easily when they stepped back. She keeps jokes about work, not people. Once she caught herself gushing at a junior and asked, "Am I being too much?" The junior laughed, "No, it's nice." I have told Ritu her warmth is a real asset to the team and asked her to keep checking, as she does.

qa.q: What did Ritu organise when Anil's proposal was approved?
qa.a: A small tea break for everyone.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she asked the junior "Am I being too much?"
qa.a: A little unsure whether her delight was welcome, which shows she cares how it lands.

qa.q: What does Ritu do that keeps warmth appropriate at work?
qa.a: She offers a namaste instead of hugs, keeps jokes about work, and checks whether her enthusiasm is welcome.

qa.q: How might the uneasy new colleague have felt when Ritu offered a namaste?
qa.a: Relieved that their step back was accepted easily.

grounding: A young adult shares delight and celebrates others' wins while keeping professional limits at work, seen and noted by a manager.

subtype: Affectionate and delighted at work and home [Regulating]
passage: Sunday, 11:20 pm. Zeenat, you shrieked in the kitchen tonight. Offices open on Sundays in our department, so this morning I nearly hugged Meena when she approved my leave. I stopped myself and just said thank you with my biggest smile, and she smiled back. Then tonight Dilnaz, my flatmate, got the scholarship email and I actually shrieked. I asked, "Can I hug you?" because she had looked tired all week. She said, "Yes, please, I've been waiting for someone to be loud about it." We made sooji halwa at 11 pm 🎉. I asked, "Should I tell the others?" and she said, "Family first, tomorrow you can tell whoever." I like being someone who cheers loudly for others, and I want it to be welcome every time.

qa.q: What did Zeenat and Dilnaz make at 11 pm?
qa.a: Sooji halwa.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she stopped herself from hugging Meena?
qa.a: Delighted about her leave but aware that a hug at work might not be welcome, so she chose a big smile.

qa.q: How did Zeenat make her joy welcome at home?
qa.a: She asked before hugging Dilnaz and asked before telling others.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz have felt about Zeenat's loud joy?
qa.a: Glad and supported, since she said she had been waiting for someone to be loud about it.

grounding: A young adult shares delight and affection at home by asking first, and keeps to professional limits at work.
